title: Root: ob- (against) — the heart, the will, the volume
core: All three are built on **ob-** ("against") and all three name a resistance that won't give way to pressure. Each locates that resistance in a different place: in the heart that won't soften, in the will that won't reverse, in the body that won't be quieted. All three are verdicts from the person being blocked — nobody calls themselves any of these.

words.nuance: The resistance is **emotional**, not intellectual: what fails to move you is pleading, pity, or the sight of suffering. **Obdurate** implies a moral failing — a hardened heart the speaker is condemning — and lives in near-biblical register (an obdurate sinner, an obdurate creditor). Wrong word for a stain or a lid; it needs someone capable of mercy who withholds it.

The resistance is to **argument and evidence**: you've been shown you're wrong and you still won't turn. **Obstinate** says nothing about your feelings, only that your will has outlasted any reason for it — you may be damaging yourself. Uniquely among these, it works on inanimate things: an obstinate cough, an obstinate lid.

The only one that makes **noise**. **Obstreperous** requires both volume and defiance — resistance you can hear from across the room — and it is always spoken downward, by whoever is supposed to be in charge (teacher, judge, flight crew). The others resist silently; this one is a scene.

exam_note: The trap is treating them as interchangeable "stubborn": check whether the sentence supplies pity being refused (obdurate), a losing argument being continued (obstinate), or actual disruptive noise (obstreperous).
